name: Loun
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Tauern, Odo D. 1928-1931. Beitrag zur Kenntnis der Sprachen und Dialekte von Seran. Anthropos 23-26 (overview/grammar sketch per Glottolog; not digitized open-access)

sources.citation: Tauern, Odo D. 1929/1930/1931. Beitrag zur Kenntnis der Sprachen und Dialekte von Seran (parts 2-4). Anthropos 24: 953-981; 25: 567-578; 26: 109-139.
sources.note: Makabala (Wakolo), Seleman and Wahinama/Manusela sketches each state penultimate stress with accent-marked exceptions; Loun does not occur in any of the three continuation parts (the 1931 'Loun' hits are the Kurnai Loun-Borun myth in another article).

sources.citation: Grimes, Charles E. & Owen Edwards. 2026. Austronesian languages of eastern Indonesia and Timor-Leste. Berlin: Language Science Press (526).
sources.note: Loun [lox] appears only in the classification tree ('Loun [lox] *b > h; **au > oi') and the language index (source Collins 1983). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Collins, James T. 2022. Language death in Indonesia: a sociocultural pandemic. Linguistik Indonesia 40(2): 141-164 (Loun at p. 156).
sources.note: Only recent account of Loun (sociolinguistic); confirms no coherent lexical data was obtainable; no phonology expected. Copy already held by the project at

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3, languoid loun1239; Wikipedia (en) 'Loun language'; Wikipedia (pl) 'Język loun' (citing Collins 2022, Linguistik Indonesia 40(2): 156, and Wurm 2007).
sources.note: Extinct; Glottolog lists no descriptive reference (only Collins 1983 for subclassification); Wikipedia: by 1978 Collins 'was unable to gather coherent and complete lexical data'. No phonology.

sources.citation: Taguchi, Yoshihiko. 1989. Lexicostatistic survey of the languages indigenous to West Seram. In W. D. Laidig (ed.), Workpapers in Indonesian Languages and Cultures 6: Maluku, 15-63. Ambon: SIL / Pattimura University.
sources.note: Loun listed '(dying)'; note 1 p. 47: 'for LOUN, we could not stop at the village of Latea where Collins mentions that there are a few speakers and we have no wordlist'. No data, no stress.

sources.citation: Collins, James T. 1983. The historical relationships of the languages of Central Maluku, Indonesia. Pacific Linguistics D-47. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Comparative; Loun grouped with Alune (Amalumute). 'Loun (now absorbed into Latea).. only three or four speakers.. survive.. with the exception of Loun, these surviving speakers proved vigorous, confident and consistent informants'; fn. 80: 'Stresemann (1927:57) says that *b > p in Loun. On the whole my fieldwork with the few surviving speakers of that language confirmed this'. Stress statements only for Hoamoal/Asilulu (p. 82f.), Kaibobo, Buru. SILENT on Loun stress.

sources.citation: Collins, James T. 1982. Linguistic research in Maluku: a report of recent field work. Oceanic Linguistics 21(1/2): 73-146.

sources.note: Collins's field report covering his 1978-80 Seram work, including the Latea/Loun visit; might record what little Loun material he got and any phonetic notes.

sources.citation: Tauern, Odo D. 1928. Beitrag zur Kenntnis der Sprachen und Dialekte von Seran (part 1). Anthropos 23(5/6): 1000-1020.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: The only first-hand description of Loun: one paragraph, p. 1019 ('Sprachen von Loun, Patunuru und Eti / Loun'): Loun said locally to derive from Manipa, contains many coastal-language words (lima, sawa, nia, pia..), plural -a/-ja, adjectives from stative verbs (mamitene, paputike, mamulane), causative a-. p. 1001: 'Ein geringeres Material sammelte ich in Eti, Loun und Patunuru.' NOTHING on stress; no accent marks on the Loun forms.
